canonical_statement: The study compared fully weight-based IV unfractionated heparin protocols with weight-based initial dosing followed by non-weight-based dosage titration for achieving therapeutic aPTT.
A secondary objective compared the two dosing approaches specifically among patients managed with the low-target aPTT protocol.
The investigators conducted a single-centre retrospective observational before-and-after study.
Both compared UFH strategies included low-target and standard-target aPTT variants; complete protocol details were referenced in Appendices 1-4 outside the retrieved PDF.
Eligible patients were older than 18 years.
Eligible patients had received therapeutic IV unfractionated heparin for any indication.

canonical_statement: At the study institution, aPTT was measured every 6 hours until therapeutic and every 24 hours thereafter.
Collected data included age, sex, weight, baseline aPTT, UFH indication, protocol target, UFH dose, all on-therapy aPTT values, and all heparin doses including the initial bolus if used.
The convenience sample was assembled by sequential chart review by date, screening enough records to obtain similar before and after group sizes.
Baseline comparisons used two-sample t tests for parametric data, Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for nonparametric data, and chi-square tests for categorical data.
Between-group analyses were adjusted for age, sex, and weight.
Poisson regression, logistic regression, and multinomial logistic regression were used for count, binary, and ordinal outcomes, respectively.
Each co-primary outcome used a significance threshold of p<0.025, corresponding to a combined primary-outcome alpha below 0.05.
Secondary outcomes used p<0.05 for significance, and analyses were performed in SAS version 9.4.
The Providence Health Care Research Institute Office of Research Ethics approved the study (H20-02807).
Of 1969 screened records, 267 patients were included in the study.
The included cohort comprised 130 patients in the non-weight-based titration group and 137 patients in the fully weight-based group.
The overall cohort had mean age 65.6 years (SD 14.0), mean weight 82.8 kg (SD 20.5), and 82 of 267 patients (30.7%) were female.

UFH indications were unstable angina/non-ST-elevation ACS in 75 patients (28.1%), ST-elevation ACS in 31 (11.6%), atrial fibrillation in 109 (40.8%), heart valve indications in 19 (7.1%), and other indications in 33 (12.4%).
Low-target protocols were used in 50.8% (66/130) of the non-weight-based titration group and 67.2% (92/137) of the fully weight-based group.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that non-weight-based dosage titration was similarly effective to fully weight-based UFH dosing for the number of adjustments to therapeutic aPTT and the proportion therapeutic at 24 hours.
The authors suggested that weight-based initial dosing may be important for achieving therapeutic aPTT, whereas weight-based dosage adjustments may be less important.
The authors proposed that the greater frequency of subtherapeutic first aPTT values with the low-target non-weight-based titration protocol might be related to its lower initial weight-based dose.
The authors stated that this was the first study comparing non-weight-based dosage titration with fully weight-based IV UFH dosing.
The retrospective observational design and small sample size created risks of bias and confounding.
The study used a convenience sample rather than a prospectively defined probability sample.

The study occurred during implementation of an EMR system, which could have biased or confounded protocol performance because of the learning curve despite exclusion of the first two implementation months.
Bleeding and thrombotic outcomes were not collected, so the study could not determine whether achieving aPTT targets was associated with clinical outcomes.
The authors reported that no funding was received.
The authors declared no competing interests.
Stephen Shalansky was an editor of the Canadian Journal of Hospital Pharmacy but was not involved in editorial decision-making for the article.
